topic.title: Moments and equilibrium of a horizontal uniform rod
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. A horizontal uniform rod has appeared every year from 2019 to 2026, as Q4, Q5 or Q6, worth 7 to 14 marks, and the reports call it a good or very good discriminator. The first marks are for the force diagram and a correctly set-up moment; the last are for the two conditions used together, with a ratio, an unknown distance or a moved load.
mustMemorise: Moment = force x perpendicular distance from the point, in N m
The weight of a uniform rod acts at its midpoint, not halfway between the supports
Equilibrium: clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments about any point, AND upward forces = downward forces
Take moments about a point where an unknown you do not want acts: it has no moment there
Two strings carry two different tensions: label them differently
On the point of tipping about one support, the reaction at the other support is zero
notOnThisSpec: Hinges and ladders: excluded by the CCEA Teacher Guidance
Non-uniform rods, whose weight does not act at the midpoint
Rods that are not horizontal, and forces at an angle to the rod
Friction at a support, and toppling against sliding
Couples, and centres of mass of composite bodies

mustBeAbleTo: Mark every force on a rod: each reaction or tension with its own label, each weight in newtons, and the rod's weight at its midpoint
Calculate a moment as force x perpendicular distance
Take moments about a chosen point, choosing one where an unknown you do not want acts
Resolve vertically: upward forces equal downward forces
Handle reactions in a given ratio by writing R and kR into both equations
Keep an unknown distance as a letter and solve the moments equation for it
Recalculate the reactions whenever a load is moved or added
Resolve vertically for equal reactions: each is half the total downward force
Keep a length you are asked to show as an unknown, with the rod's weight at half of it
Set the reaction at the far support to zero when a rod is on the point of tipping
sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, g = 10 m/s². A uniform rod appears every year, usually as Q4, Q5 or Q6, worth 7 to 14 marks: a force diagram (2), then the reactions or tensions, often with a ratio, an unknown distance or a changed load. Schemes give M1 for taking moments about a point, MW1 for each correct side of the moments equation and W1 for the value, then MW1 and W1 for resolving vertically; a single correct moment usually earns a mark even inside a wrong equation.
traps: Both strings given one letter, given weights dropped, reactions added, and the rod's weight drawn halfway between the strings instead of at its midpoint (Summer 2019 Q4)
R and 3R mishandled; moments used where resolving vertically was needed; g left out; the reaction not recalculated after the load moved; the plank's weight omitted (Summer 2022 Q6)
Moments taken about A, B, C and the centre at random, with labels given as masses and the rod's weight left off (Summer 2023 Q5)
The same diagram faults again, with moments about every point on the rod seen; any correct moment still earned a mark (Summer 2024 Q5)
Reactions added at A and B where there are none, and trial and error instead of an equation in the unknown distance d (Summer 2025 Q5)

workedExamples.stem:
A uniform plank AB, of length 6 m and weight 250 N, rests horizontally on two trestles, one at A and one at C, where AC = 5 m. A child of weight 400 N stands on the plank at D, where AD = 4 m. The plank is in equilibrium.

(i) Calculate the reaction at C.
(ii) Calculate the reaction at A.

steps.working:
The plank is uniform, so its 250 N weight acts at its midpoint.
Distance from A $= 3$ m
steps.decision: Put the rod's own weight in first, at the midpoint. Forgetting it is the error the reports record most often on this question.

options: Because a uniform plank's weight acts at its midpoint
Because the weight acts halfway between the trestles
Because the weight acts at the heavier end
whyMenu.explain: "Uniform" means the mass is spread evenly, so the weight acts at the middle of the plank, 3 m from A. Halfway between the trestles, 2.5 m, is the misplacement the 2019 report names.

steps.working:
$5R_C = 250 \times 3 + 400 \times 4$
$5R_C = 750 + 1600$
Moments about A, so the reaction at A drops out.
steps.decision: Take moments about A because $R_A$ acts there: its distance is zero, so it drops out and leaves one unknown. Each weight turns the plank clockwise about A; $R_C$ turns it anticlockwise.
Work out each moment separately before adding, so a slip is easy to find.
With one reaction known, up equals down gives the other in one line. Check it with moments about C if there is time.

(i) Calculate the tension in the string at D.
(ii) Calculate the tension in the string at C.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.working: Weights: 50 N at A, 40 N at the midpoint (1.5 m from A) and 70 N at B. The tensions are $T_C$ and $T_D$.
steps.decision: Two strings means two different tensions, so give them different letters. Every mass becomes a weight before it goes near an equation.

options: Because the two strings generally carry different tensions
Because tension is always labelled T
whyMenu.explain: One letter for both strings would say they pull equally, which they do not here. The 2024 report records exactly this labelling error.

steps.working:
$2T_D + 50 \times 0.4 = 40 \times 1.1 + 70 \times 2.6$
$2T_D + 20 = 44 + 182$
Moments about C, so the tension at C drops out.
steps.decision: About C, $T_C$ drops out. Measure every distance from C: the mass at A is on the other side of C, so its moment is anticlockwise, on the same side of the equation as $T_D$.
Collect the numbers, then divide by the distance from C to D.
Up equals down finishes it. The strings carry the whole weight between them, the rod's included.

workedExamples.stem:
A uniform plank AB, of length 4 m and mass 15 kg, rests horizontally on two supports at C and D, where AC = DB = 1 m. A child of mass 30 kg stands on the plank.

(i) The child stands at the midpoint of the plank. Calculate the reaction at each support.
(ii) The child walks towards B. Calculate how far beyond D she can stand before the plank starts to tip.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 137' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='137'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='46' y='57' width='308' height='14' rx='3' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.1' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M123 71l-11 21h22Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><path d='M277 71l-11 21h22Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><rect x='287.8' y='29' width='55.5' height='28' rx='3' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='315.5' y='48' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>30 kg</text><text x='38' y='70' text-anchor='end' font-size='16' font-weight='600'>A</text><text x='110' y='88' text-anchor='end' font-size='16' font-weight='600'>C</text><text x='264' y='88' text-anchor='end' font-size='16' font-weight='600'>D</text><text x='362' y='70' text-anchor='start' font-size='16' font-weight='600'>B</text><path d='M200 120v10M277 120v10M200 125H277' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.1' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='238.5' y='118' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14'>1 m</text><path d='M277 120v10M315.5 120v10M277 125H315.5' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.1' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='296.3' y='118' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14'>x</text></g></svg>

steps.working: (i) Both weights act at the midpoint, halfway between C and D, so the supports share them equally: each reaction is $\frac{150 + 300}{2} = 225$ N.
steps.decision: Symmetry is a legitimate shortcut here, and moments about C confirm it: $2R_D = 450 \times 1$.

steps.working: (ii) On the point of tipping about D, the plank only just touches C, so $R_C = 0$.
steps.decision: This is the one idea the tipping part tests. Setting the reaction at C to zero leaves a single unknown, the child's distance beyond D.

options: Because the plank is about to lift off C
Because the child is standing beyond D
whyMenu.explain: As the child walks out, the plank presses less and less on C. At the moment it starts to tip it presses not at all, so the reaction there has fallen to zero.

steps.working:
Taking moments about D:
$150 \times 1 = 300x$
Distance beyond D: $x = 0.5$ m
steps.decision: Take moments about D, the support it tips about: the plank's weight turns it one way, the child the other, and $R_D$ has no moment there.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (i) 225 N at each support  (ii) 0.5 m beyond D

twin.stem: A uniform plank AB, of length 5 m and mass 20 kg, rests on supports at C and D, where AC = DB = 1 m. A person of mass 50 kg walks from D towards B. How far beyond D, in metres, can they stand before the plank tips? Take $g = 10$ m/s².

items.stem: From an earlier topic: what is the weight of a 7 kg mass, taking $g = 10$ m/s²?

options.feedback: That is the mass with a newton sign on it; the weight is $mg$.
That divides by $g$ instead of multiplying.
That adds $g$ rather than multiplying by it.
That is $4R$; there is still a division by 4 to do.
That multiplies by 4 instead of dividing.
Work out each product first: $3 \times 50 = 150$ and $2 \times 40 = 80$, then add.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a lamp hangs at rest from two vertical cords with tensions 14 N and 26 N. What is the weight of the lamp?

options.feedback: At rest, up equals down: $14 + 26 = 40$ N.
Both cords pull up, so their tensions add.
That averages the tensions; the weight is their total.
That is one cord's pull. Both cords hold the lamp up.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: $R + 3R = 240$. What is $R$?

options.feedback: That divides by 3. $R$ and $3R$ together make four lots of $R$.
That halves 240, as though the two terms were equal.
That multiplies by 3; the equation asks for a division.

items.skill: Where a uniform rod's weight acts
items.stem: A uniform rod rests on two supports that are not symmetrically placed. Where does the rod's weight act?

options.text: At the midpoint of the rod
options.feedback: Uniform means evenly spread, so the weight acts at the middle of the rod, wherever the supports are.
The supports do not move the rod's weight. The 2019 report records many candidates drawing it here, between the strings.

options.text: At the support nearer the middle
options.feedback: The weight acts at the rod's midpoint, which need not be at either support.

options.text: It can be left out, because the supports carry it
options.feedback: The supports do carry it, which is exactly why it must be in the equations: leave it out and every reaction comes out too small.

items.stem: A uniform rod AB is 2 m long and rests on a pivot at C, where AC = 0.6 m. A 50 N force acts vertically downwards at A. What is its moment about C?

options.feedback: $50 \times 0.6 = 30$ N m: the force times its distance from C.
That uses 1.4 m, the distance from B. A moment about C uses the distance from C.
That uses the rod's whole length. Only the distance from C to the force counts.

items.stem: A uniform rod rests in equilibrium on two supports. Which statement is true?

options.text: Moments about any point balance, and the upward forces equal the downward forces
options.feedback: Both hold at once, and a full answer usually needs both.

options.text: Only the moments need to balance
options.feedback: The vertical forces balance as well, and that equation is often the quicker way to a reaction.

options.text: Only the vertical forces need to balance
options.feedback: Up equals down gives the total of the reactions, but not how they are shared; the moments decide that.

items.stem: A rod rests on supports at C and D. You want the reaction at D and do not know the reaction at C. About which point should you take moments?

options.feedback: About C the reaction at C has no distance, so it drops out and $R_D$ is the only unknown.
About D, the reaction you want has no moment, so it vanishes from the equation instead.
About the midpoint both reactions stay in the equation, so it has two unknowns.

items.stem: The reaction at C is three times as large as the reaction at A, and the total downward force on the rod is 200 N. What is the reaction at A?

options.feedback: That divides by 3. $R$ and $3R$ make four lots of $R$.
That shares the 200 N equally, ignoring the ratio.
That is the reaction at C, three quarters of the total.

items.stem: A box on a plank resting on two supports is moved closer to one of them. Which is true?

options.text: Both reactions change, so both must be recalculated
options.feedback: The total is unchanged, but moments decide how it is shared, and a moved box changes the moments.

options.text: The reactions stay the same, because the total weight has not changed
options.feedback: Only their total stays the same. The 2022 report records candidates reusing the old reaction here.

options.text: Only the reaction at the nearer support changes
options.feedback: If one changes, the other must change by the same amount the other way, because the total is fixed.

items.stem: A rod hangs from two vertical strings at C and D. How should the tensions be labelled?

options.text: With different letters, such as $T_C$ and $T_D$
options.feedback: Each string carries its own tension, and they are usually different.
One letter says the two strings pull equally, which is rarely true. The 2024 report records this labelling error.

options.text: Both $\frac{W}{2}$, because the strings share the weight
options.feedback: They share it equally only in a symmetrical set-up. In general the moments decide the split.

items.stem: Taking moments gives $300d = 1020$, where $d$ is a distance in metres. What should you do next?

options.feedback: It is an ordinary linear equation, and one division solves it.

options.text: Try values of $d$ until both sides agree
options.feedback: Trial and error costs time and rarely lands exactly. The 2025 report saw the weakest candidates do this instead of solving.
Diagrams are not drawn to scale, so the distance has to come from the equation.

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB is 5 m long.

How far from A does the rod's weight act?

Answer ________ m
hints: Uniform means the mass is spread evenly along the rod.
parts.workedSolution: The rod is uniform, so its weight acts at its midpoint, $5 \div 2 = 2.5$ m from A.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the far end of the rod. A uniform rod's weight acts at its midpoint, halfway along: 2.5 m from A.

context.setting: The moment of a hanging mass

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB, of length 3 m, rests on a pivot at C, where AC = 0.8 m. A mass of 6 kg hangs from the end A.

What is the moment of the mass's weight about C?

Answer ________

options.feedback: The weight is $6 \times 10 = 60$ N and its distance from C is 0.8 m, so the moment is $60 \times 0.8 = 48$ N m.
That multiplies the mass, 6 kg, by the distance. A moment needs the weight in newtons: $6 \times 10 = 60$ N first.
That uses 2.2 m, the distance from B. A moment about C uses the distance from C to the force, which is 0.8 m.
That uses the rod's whole length. Only the distance from C to the line of the force counts.

hints: Turn the mass into a weight first.
Measure the distance from C, the point the moment is about.
parts.workedSolution: The weight is $6 \times 10 = 60$ N, acting 0.8 m from C, so its moment about C is $60 \times 0.8 = 48$ N m, anticlockwise.

context.setting: A see-saw in balance

parts.stem:
A uniform plank of length 4 m rests on a pivot at its midpoint. Aoife, of mass 45 kg, sits 1.6 m from the pivot. Ciarán, of mass 60 kg, sits on the other side so that the plank balances horizontally.

Calculate Ciarán's distance from the pivot.

Answer ________ m
hints: The plank's own weight acts at the pivot, so it has no moment about the pivot.
Clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.
parts.workedSolution: Moments about the pivot: $450 \times 1.6 = 600x$, so $720 = 600x$ and $x = 1.2$ m. The plank's weight acts at the pivot and has no moment there.

commonErrors.feedback: Your equation was right, but 0.8 m is Ciarán's distance from the end of the plank. The question asks for his distance from the pivot, 1.2 m.
That is Ciarán's distance from the far end of the plank, where Aoife's side begins. Moments are about the pivot, so the distance asked for is measured from the pivot: 1.2 m.

context.setting: A beam on two supports with a load

parts.stem:
A uniform beam AB, of length 5 m and mass 30 kg, rests horizontally on supports at A and B. A load of mass 20 kg rests on the beam 1.5 m from A.

By taking moments about A, calculate the reaction at B.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: The beam's own weight acts at its midpoint.
About A, the reaction at A has no moment.
parts.workedSolution: Moments about A: $5R_B = 300 \times 2.5 + 200 \times 1.5 = 1050$, so $R_B = 210$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The beam's own weight is missing. It is 300 N acting at the midpoint, 2.5 m from A, and it turns the beam just as the load does.
That measures the load's distance from B, 3.5 m, which is what moments about B need, and moments about B give the reaction at A. About A, every distance is measured from A.
The method is right, but the masses went in as 30 and 20 instead of weights. Multiply each by $g = 10$ to get newtons.

context.setting: A beam on two supports with a load

parts.stem:
A uniform beam AB, of length 5 m and mass 30 kg, rests horizontally on supports at A and B. A load of mass 20 kg rests on the beam 1.5 m from A, and the reaction at B is 210 N.

Calculate the reaction at A.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: One reaction is known, so resolve vertically.
Up equals down: the two reactions carry the beam and the load.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $R_A + 210 = 300 + 200$, so $R_A = 290$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The load's 200 N is missing from the downward forces. The two reactions hold up the beam and the load together: $R_A + 210 = 300 + 200$.
That is the whole downward force, as though A held everything up. The support at B carries 210 N of it, so take that off: $R_A = 300 + 200 - 210$.

context.setting: Two supports sharing a plank in a given ratio

parts.stem:
A uniform plank of mass 24 kg rests horizontally on two supports. One support pushes up three times as hard as the other.

Calculate the smaller reaction.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: Call the smaller reaction $R$; the other is then $3R$.
Up equals down.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $R + 3R = 240$, so $4R = 240$ and $R = 60$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides by 3. The two reactions are $R$ and $3R$, which make $4R$ between them, so divide by 4.
That shares the weight equally, which ignores the ratio. Write the reactions as $R$ and $3R$ before resolving.
The ratio is handled correctly, but the plank's mass, 24 kg, went in where its weight, 240 N, belongs.

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB, of length 2.4 m and mass 3 kg, hangs horizontally from two vertical strings attached at C and D, where AC = 0.3 m and DB = 0.6 m. A mass of 3 kg hangs from A and a mass of 4 kg hangs from B.

Calculate the tension in the string at D.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: About C, the tension at C has no moment.
The mass at A is on the other side of C from B, so its moment turns the rod the other way.
parts.workedSolution: Moments about C: $1.5T_D + 30 \times 0.3 = 30 \times 0.9 + 40 \times 2.1$, so $1.5T_D + 9 = 111$ and $T_D = 68$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The rod's own weight, 30 N at its midpoint, 0.9 m from C, is missing from the moments. It is the force the reports record being left out most often.
The distances were measured from A, but the moments are about C. From C, the rod's weight is 0.9 m away, B is 2.1 m away, and the mass at A, 0.3 m away on the other side, has a moment too.
The mass at A hangs on the other side of C, so its moment turns the rod anticlockwise, the same way as $T_D$. It belongs with $T_D$, not added to the clockwise moments.

context.setting: A rod hung from two strings

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB, of length 2.4 m and mass 3 kg, hangs horizontally from two vertical strings attached at C and D. A mass of 3 kg hangs from A and a mass of 4 kg hangs from B. The tension in the string at D is 68 N.

Calculate the tension in the string at C.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: With one tension known, resolve vertically.
The two strings hold up the rod and both masses.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $T_C + 68 = 30 + 30 + 40$, so $T_C = 32$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The rod's own 30 N is missing from the downward forces. The strings hold up the rod as well as the two masses.
That gives the string at C the same tension as the string at D. Two strings carry two different tensions; up equals down gives this one.

context.setting: A rod resting on supports that are not at its ends

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB, of length 5 m and mass 8 kg, rests horizontally on two supports, one at A and one at C, where AC = 3 m.

Calculate the reaction at C.

Take $g = 10$ m/s². Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Where does the weight of a uniform rod act?
It is not halfway between the supports.
parts.workedSolution: The weight acts at the midpoint, 2.5 m from A. Moments about A: $3R_C = 80 \times 2.5 = 200$, so $R_C = 66.67$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That puts the weight halfway between the supports, 1.5 m from A. A uniform rod's weight acts at the rod's own midpoint, 2.5 m from A, wherever the supports are. The 2019 report names this misplacement.
That is the reaction at A. Taking moments about C removes the reaction at C from the equation, so it can only give $R_A$. To find $R_C$, take moments about A.

context.setting: Where a person stands on a plank, from the ratio of the reactions

parts.stem:
A uniform plank AB, of length 4 m and mass 20 kg, rests horizontally on supports at A and B. A person of mass 40 kg stands on the plank at P. The reaction at B is twice the reaction at A.

Calculate the distance AP.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ m
hints: Call the reaction at A $R$, so the reaction at B is $2R$, and resolve vertically first.
Then take moments about A with AP as the unknown.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $R + 2R = 600$, so $R = 200$ N and the reaction at B is 400 N. Moments about A: $400 \times 4 = 200 \times 2 + 400 \times AP$, so $1200 = 400 \times AP$ and $AP = 3$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That uses the ratio the wrong way round, putting 200 N at B. The question says the reaction at B is the larger one, twice the reaction at A, so $R_B = 400$ N.
The plank's own weight is missing from both equations: from the vertical total and from the moments. It is 200 N acting at the midpoint, 2 m from A.

A uniform rod AB, of length 6 m and mass 10 kg, hangs horizontally from a single vertical string attached to the rod at C, where AC = $d$ m. A mass of 8 kg hangs from A and a mass of 12 kg hangs from B.

Calculate the tension in the string.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: One string holds everything up.
Up equals down.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $T = 80 + 100 + 120 = 300$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The rod's own 100 N is missing. The string holds up the rod as well as the two masses.
That adds the masses in kilograms. The tension is a force, so each mass becomes a weight first: multiply by 10.

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB, of length 6 m and mass 10 kg, hangs horizontally from a single vertical string attached to the rod at C, where AC = $d$ m. A mass of 8 kg hangs from A and a mass of 12 kg hangs from B. The tension in the string is 300 N.

Calculate the value of $d$.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________
hints: Take moments about A, where the mass at A has no moment.
Keep $d$ in the equation and solve it; do not guess.
parts.workedSolution: Moments about A: $300d = 100 \times 3 + 120 \times 6 = 1020$, so $d = 3.4$.

commonErrors.feedback: The rod's own weight, 100 N at 3 m from A, has no moment in your equation. About A it turns the rod clockwise along with the mass at B.
That is the distance BC. The question defines $d$ as AC, the distance from A, so $d = 3.4$.

context.setting: A box moved along a plank

parts.stem:
A uniform plank AB, of length 4 m and mass 20 kg, rests horizontally on supports at A and B. A box of mass 30 kg sits on the plank 1 m from A, and the reaction at B is 175 N. The box is then moved to a point 2.5 m from A.

Calculate the new reaction at B.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: taking moments about A with the box in its new position

hints: A new position means new moments.
Take moments about A again, from scratch.
parts.workedSolution: Moments about A with the box moved: $4R_B = 200 \times 2 + 300 \times 2.5 = 1150$, so $R_B = 287.5$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reaction before the box moved. Moving the box changes its moment, so the reaction has to be worked out again. The 2022 report records this reuse.
The new position is used correctly, but the plank's own weight, 200 N at the midpoint, has dropped out of the moments. The 2022 report records the plank's weight omitted in exactly this part.

context.setting: Which equation answers which question

parts.stem:
A uniform rod rests on two pivots. Both reactions are known, and an unknown mass $M$ kg hangs from one end.

Which is the most direct way to find $M$?

Answer ________

options.text: Resolve vertically: the two reactions equal the rod's weight plus $Mg$
options.feedback: One equation, one unknown: up equals down gives $M$ straight away.

options.text: Take moments about the end where the mass hangs
options.feedback: About that end, the mass has no moment, so $M$ does not appear in the equation at all.

options.text: Take moments about the midpoint of the rod
options.feedback: That can work, but it needs every distance right. The 2022 report records this route producing many incorrect equations where resolving was all that was needed.

hints: Which equation contains $M$ and nothing else unknown?
parts.workedSolution: Both reactions are known, so the vertical equation has one unknown: the reactions add up to the rod's weight plus $Mg$. Resolving vertically finds $M$ directly.

context.setting: Every force on a rod hung from two strings

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB hangs horizontally from two vertical strings at C and D, with a 5 kg mass at A and a 7 kg mass at B.

Which list gives every force acting on the rod, labelled correctly?

Answer ________

options.text: Tensions $T_C$ and $T_D$ up; 50 N at A, 70 N at B and the rod's weight at its midpoint, all down
options.feedback: Two tensions with their own labels, and three weights: the two masses' and the rod's own, at its midpoint.

options.text: Tensions $T$ and $T$ up; 50 N at A, 70 N at B and the rod's weight at its midpoint, all down
options.feedback: Two strings need two letters: one letter says they pull equally. The 2024 report records this labelling error.

options.text: Tensions $T_C$ and $T_D$ up, and reactions up at A and B; 50 N at A, 70 N at B and the rod's weight, all down
options.feedback: There is nothing at A or B to push up: the rod is held only by the strings. The 2023 and 2025 reports record these extra reactions.

options.text: Tensions $T_C$ and $T_D$ up; 50 N at A and 70 N at B down
options.feedback: The rod's own weight is missing. A uniform rod's weight acts at its midpoint and must be marked.

options.text: Tensions $T_C$ and $T_D$ up; 5 kg at A, 7 kg at B and the rod's weight at its midpoint, all down
options.feedback: Forces are weights in newtons, not masses in kilograms. The reports record labels given as masses.

scheme.for: all five forces correctly labelled and directed

hints: Count the strings, and count the weights, the rod's own included.
parts.workedSolution: Two tensions, $T_C$ and $T_D$, act up; three weights act down: 50 N at A, 70 N at B and the rod's own weight at its midpoint.

context.setting: How far out before a plank tips

parts.stem:
A uniform plank AB, of length 5 m and mass 30 kg, rests horizontally on two supports at C and D, where AC = DB = 1 m. A boy of mass 50 kg walks along the plank from D towards B.

Calculate how far beyond D he can stand before the plank starts to tip.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: on the point of tipping about D, the reaction at C is zero

hints: When the plank is about to tip about D, what is the reaction at C?
Take moments about D.
parts.workedSolution: On the point of tipping about D the reaction at C is zero. Moments about D: $300 \times 1.5 = 500x$, so $x = 0.9$ m beyond D.

commonErrors.feedback: That uses 2.5 m, the plank's weight measured from A. The moments are about D, so the plank's weight is 1.5 m from D.
Your moments are right, but 4.9 m is the boy's distance from A. The question asks how far beyond D he stands: 0.9 m.

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB, of length 4 m and mass 6 kg, is held horizontally by two light, vertical strings attached to the rod at C and D, where AC = 0.5 m and DB = 1 m. A mass of 5 kg is attached at A and a mass of 8 kg is attached at B. The rod is in equilibrium.

Calculate the tension in the string at D.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: Every mass becomes a weight, and the rod's weight acts at its midpoint.
About C, the tension at C drops out.
parts.workedSolution: Weights: 50 N at A, 60 N at the midpoint and 80 N at B. Moments about C: $2.5T_D + 50 \times 0.5 = 60 \times 1.5 + 80 \times 3.5$, so $2.5T_D + 25 = 370$ and $T_D = 138$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The rod's own weight is missing: 60 N at its midpoint, 1.5 m from C. The 2024 report names this as the commonest omission on this question.
The distances were measured from A while the moments were taken about C. From C, the midpoint is 1.5 m away, B is 3.5 m away and A is 0.5 m away on the other side.
The weight at A is on the other side of C, so its moment is anticlockwise, like $T_D$'s. Adding it to the clockwise moments counts it the wrong way.
The shape of the moments equation is right, but the masses went in as kilograms. A tension is a force: use weights, multiplying each mass by 10.

parts.stem:
Calculate the tension in the string at C.

Answer ________ N
hints: With $T_D$ known, resolve vertically.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $T_C + 138 = 50 + 60 + 80 = 190$, so $T_C = 52$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That shares the 190 N equally between the strings, as though both carried the same tension $T$. The strings are at different places, so their tensions differ: $T_C = 190 - T_D$.

parts.stem:
A uniform plank AB, of length 4.5 m and mass 16 kg, rests horizontally on two pivots, one at A and one at C, where AC = 4 m. A box of mass 20 kg is placed on the plank at P, between A and C. The reaction at C is three times as large as the reaction at A.

Calculate the reaction at A.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: Call the reaction at A $R$, so the reaction at C is $3R$.
Up equals down.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $R + 3R = 160 + 200$, so $4R = 360$ and $R = 90$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides by 3. With $R$ at A and $3R$ at C, the two reactions make $4R$, so $4R = 360$. The 2022 report records candidates unable to handle $R$ and $3R$.
The ratio is handled well, but the plank's own weight, 160 N, is missing from the total the pivots carry.

parts.stem:
Calculate the distance AP.

Answer ________ m
hints: The reaction at C is three times as large as the reaction at A: 270 N.
Take moments about A and keep AP as the unknown.
parts.workedSolution: The reaction at C is $3 \times 90 = 270$ N. Moments about A: $270 \times 4 = 160 \times 2.25 + 200 \times AP$, so $1080 = 360 + 200 \times AP$ and $AP = 3.6$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: The plank's own weight has no moment in your equation. It is 160 N at the midpoint, 2.25 m from A, and without it P lands beyond the end of the plank. The 2022 report records the plank's weight omitted.
That puts $R$, 90 N, at C. The reaction at C is $3R = 270$ N; the ratio has to go into the moments equation as well as the vertical one.

parts.stem:
The box is moved to the end B, and the plank stays horizontal and in equilibrium.

Calculate the new reaction at C.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: taking moments about A with the box at B

hints: The box has moved, so the reactions are no longer $R$ and $3R$: find them again.
Take moments about A.
parts.workedSolution: With the box at B, moments about A: $4R_C = 160 \times 2.25 + 200 \times 4.5 = 1260$, so $R_C = 315$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reaction at C before the box moved. The ratio of three to one belonged to the old position; a moved box needs new moments. The 2022 report records this exact reuse.
The box's new moment is right, but the plank's own weight is missing: 160 N at 2.25 m from A.

parts.stem:
Calculate the new reaction at A.

Answer ________ N
hints: Resolve vertically with the new reaction at C.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $R_A + 315 = 160 + 200$, so $R_A = 45$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reaction at A from before the box moved. With the box at B, more of the weight goes to C and less to A.

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB, of length 4 m and mass 3 kg, rests horizontally in equilibrium on a single pivot at C, where AC = $x$ m. A mass of 4 kg is attached at A and a mass of 1 kg is attached at B.

Calculate the reaction at the pivot.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: The pivot holds up everything.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $R = 40 + 30 + 10 = 80$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The rod's own weight, 30 N, is missing. The 2023 report records the rod's weight omitted on exactly this question shape.

parts.stem:
Calculate the value of $x$.

Answer ________
hints: Take moments about A, where the mass at A has no moment.
Keep $x$ as a letter and solve.
parts.workedSolution: Moments about A: $80x = 30 \times 2 + 10 \times 4 = 100$, so $x = 1.25$.

commonErrors.feedback: The rod's weight has no moment in your equation. About A it is 30 N at 2 m, turning the rod the same way as the mass at B.
That is the distance BC. The question defines $x$ as AC, measured from A.

parts.stem:
A further mass of 2 kg is attached at B. The pivot is moved so that the rod again rests horizontally in equilibrium.

Calculate the new distance AC.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: taking moments about A with the new masses

hints: The pivot now carries more weight: find the new reaction first.
Then take moments about A again.
parts.workedSolution: The reaction is now $40 + 30 + 30 = 100$ N. Moments about A: $100x = 30 \times 2 + 30 \times 4 = 180$, so $x = 1.8$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: The new moments are right, but they are divided by the old reaction, 80 N. The extra 2 kg adds 20 N, so the pivot now carries 100 N.
The rod's own weight has dropped out of the moments: 30 N at 2 m from A.

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB, of length 5 m and mass 12 kg, rests horizontally on two pivots, one at A and one at C, where CB = 1 m. A mass of $M$ kg hangs from B, and the rod is in equilibrium. The reaction at C is 3 times as large as the reaction at A.

Use moments about B to calculate the reaction at C.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: Write the reactions as $R$ at A and $3R$ at C.
About B the mass at B has no moment, and M disappears with it.
parts.workedSolution: About B: $5R + 1 \times 3R = 120 \times 2.5$, so $8R = 300$ and $R = 37.5$ N. The reaction at C is $3 \times 37.5 = 112.5$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $R$, the reaction at A. The part asks for the reaction at C, which is 3 times as large: $3 \times 37.5 = 112.5$ N.
That measures the reaction at C from A instead of from B. About B, C is only 1 m away, so its moment is $1 \times 3R$, not $4 \times 3R$.

parts.stem:
Calculate the value of $M$.

Answer ________
hints: Both reactions are known now, so resolve vertically.
The mass at B has weight $10M$ newtons.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving vertically: $37.5 + 112.5 = 120 + 10M$, so $10M = 30$ and $M = 3$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass's weight in newtons, $10M$. The part asks for $M$ in kilograms, so divide by $g = 10$.
That sets the two reactions equal to the weight of the mass alone. They hold up the rod's own 120 N as well: $R + 3R = 120 + 10M$.

parts.stem:
The mass at B is removed and a mass of 10 kg is hung from the rod at D, where AD = $x$ m. The rod stays horizontal, and the two reactions are now equal.

Calculate the reaction at A.

Answer ________ N
hints: Equal reactions: call each one $X$.
Resolve vertically.
parts.workedSolution: The reactions are equal, so $2X = 120 + 100 = 220$ and $X = 110$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reaction at A from before the change. The load is different now and the reactions are equal, so resolve vertically again: $2X = 220$.
The rod's own 120 N is missing: the two reactions hold up the rod as well as the new mass. $2X = 120 + 100$.

parts.stem:
Calculate the value of $x$.

Answer ________
hints: Take moments about A, so the reaction at A drops out.
Keep $x$ as a letter and solve.

commonErrors.feedback: The rod's own weight is missing from the moments: 120 N at 2.5 m from A. The 2022 report found the plank's weight omitted in exactly this part.
Your moments are right, but that is the distance from B. The question defines $x$ as AD, measured from A.

methodLock.instruction: Use moments about B to calculate the reaction at C
methodLock.requiredMethod: Take moments about B as the stem says, with the reactions written as R and 3R; the Summer 2022 report reads the named point as help (about B the unknown mass has no moment), and the scheme's marks are laid out for that equation.

A 2 kilogram mass hangs from the rod at C, 1.8 metres from A.

parts.stem:
A uniform rod AB, of length 2.4 m and mass 3 kg, hangs horizontally from two light, vertical strings. The string at A is fixed to the ceiling. The string at B passes over a smooth pulley fixed to the ceiling and carries a block of mass $m$ kg, which hangs freely. A mass of 2 kg hangs from the rod at C, where AC = 1.8 m. The system is at rest.

Calculate the value of $m$.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________

scheme.for: the tension in the string at B is the block's weight, $10m$ (the block is at rest, and the string passes over a smooth pulley)
a moments equation, e.g. about A: $2.4T_B = 30 \times 1.2 + 20 \times 1.8$

hints: The block hangs at rest. What does that make the tension in its string?
Take moments about A: the tension at A has no moment there.
parts.workedSolution: The block is at rest, so the tension in its string equals its weight, $10m$ N, and a light string over a smooth pulley carries that tension to B unchanged. About A: $2.4T_B = 30 \times 1.2 + 20 \times 1.8$, so $2.4T_B = 72$ and $T_B = 30$ N. So $10m = 30$ and $m = 3$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the tension at B, 30 N, handed in as the mass. The moments are right, so those marks (M) stand; the block hangs at rest, so its weight, $10m$, equals the tension: $m = 30 \div 10$.
That leaves the rod's own weight out of the moments. A uniform rod's 30 N acts at its midpoint, 1.2 m from A, and it turns the rod as surely as the load does.

That measures the load's distance from B, 0.6 m, in an equation about A (the same number comes out as the tension at A). Every distance in a moments equation is measured from the point the moments are about: the load is 1.8 m from A.
That makes the string at B hold up everything, as if the string at A were not there. Both strings share the load, so resolving alone cannot split it: moments about A give the share at B.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh is finding the reaction at A for a uniform plank AB, of length 4 m and weight 120 N, resting on supports at A and B, with a 200 N box 1 m from B. She calls the reaction at A $R$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 leaves out the plank's own weight. The plank is uniform, so its 120 N acts at its midpoint, 2 m from B, and it turns the plank about B just as the box does.
findTheMistake.feedback: Choosing B was exactly right: it removes the reaction at B and earns the method mark (M). The plank's own weight is the force the 2022, 2023 and 2024 reports all record being left out. Put it on the diagram first, at the midpoint, before writing any moment.

findTheMistake.stem: Tomás is finding the tension $T$ in the string at D for a uniform rod AB, of length 2 m and weight 20 N, hung from strings at C and D, where AC = 0.4 m and AD = 1.4 m. A 30 N weight hangs from A and a 20 N weight from B. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 takes moments about C but measures the distances from A. From C, the rod's weight is 0.6 m away and B is 1.6 m away, and the 30 N at A, 0.4 m on the other side of C, turns the rod the other way.
findTheMistake.feedback: Choosing C was right, and it earns the method mark (M). Once the point is chosen, every distance is measured from it. Drawing a bracket from C to each force on the diagram makes the right distances hard to miss.

findTheMistake.stem: Orla has a uniform plank AB, of length 4 m and weight 200 N, on supports at A and B. With a 400 N box 1 m from A, the reaction at A was 400 N. The box is moved to 3.5 m from A, and she finds the new reaction at B, calling it $R$. Her working:
studentWorking: The box is moved to 3.5 m from A
The reaction at A is still 400 N
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 keeps the old reaction at A. Moving the box changes its moment, so the way the weight is shared between the supports changes too; only the total, 600 N, stays the same. Take moments about A again with the box in its new place.
correction: The box is moved to 3.5 m from A
findTheMistake.feedback: Line 3 resolves vertically correctly, and on the right reaction it would earn its mark. The 2022 report records this part as one only the strongest candidates got right: a new position means new moments before anything else.

prompts.prompt: What is the moment of a force about a point?
prompts.answer: The force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the force's line of action, measured in N m.

prompts.prompt: Where does the weight of a uniform rod act?
prompts.answer: At the midpoint of the rod, wherever the supports are.

prompts.prompt: What are the two conditions for a rod in equilibrium?
prompts.answer: Moments about any point balance, clockwise equal to anticlockwise, and the upward forces equal the downward forces.

prompts.prompt: About which point should you take moments?
prompts.answer: About a point where an unknown force you do not need acts, so that force has no moment and drops out.

prompts.prompt: A rod hangs from two strings. Do the two tensions get the same letter?
prompts.answer: No: each string has its own tension, usually different, so give them different letters.

prompts.prompt: One reaction is three times the other. How do you write them?
prompts.answer: As R and 3R, and put both into both equations: there is only one unknown.

prompts.prompt: A load is moved along the rod. What must you do before using the reactions again?
prompts.answer: Recalculate them: a new position gives new moments, so new reactions.

prompts.prompt: A rod is on the point of tipping about one support. What is the reaction at the other support?
prompts.answer: Zero: the rod is only just touching it.

prompts.prompt: A distance along the rod is unknown. What do you do?
prompts.answer: Call it d, write the moments equation with d in it and solve the equation; never guess values.

prompts.prompt: What does the Unit 2 formula sheet give you for moments?
prompts.answer: Nothing: moment equals force times perpendicular distance has to be remembered.

prompts.prompt: After a change, the two reactions on a rod are equal. How do you find each one?
prompts.answer: Resolve vertically: twice the reaction equals the total downward force, so each reaction is half of it.

prompts.prompt: A part asks you to show that a rod has a given length. How do you treat the length in the moments equation?
prompts.answer: As an unknown, L, with the rod's weight at half of L: the equation must produce the given length, never start from it.

findings.asked: A uniform rod hung from two strings with masses at its ends: the forces on it, then both tensions.
findings.wentWrong: A strong discriminator. Diagrams gave both strings one letter, dropped given weights or added reactions, and put the rod's weight halfway between the strings; many earned only one mark for a moments equation with two correct moments and one for resolving vertically.
findings.rule: Each string its own tension; the rod's weight at its midpoint; every moment about the chosen point, then up = down.

findings.asked: Forces on a supported plank; moments about a point; then a changed load.
findings.wentWrong: Extra reaction at B; R and 3R mishandled; moments used where vertical equilibrium was needed; g omitted; the reaction not recalculated before the second moments equation; the plank's weight omitted.
findings.rule: Resolve vertically for the reactions; take moments about a support; include the rod's weight at its centre.

findings.asked: Diagram of a rod on one pivot, then moments to find an unknown distance.
findings.wentWrong: Rod's weight omitted; labels given as mass not weight; arrows missing; extra reactions at A and B; moments taken about various points with mixed success.
findings.rule: Choose the point that eliminates the unknown you do not want.

findings.asked: Forces on a rod hung from two strings; moments.
findings.wentWrong: Same diagram faults: weight omitted, mass labels, no arrows, extra reactions, both strings labelled with one letter; moments about every point seen, though most earned a mark for any correct moment.
findings.rule: Each string: its own tension; the rod's weight at the midpoint.

findings.asked: Diagram; a simple equilibrium; a moments equation in an unknown distance d.
findings.wentWrong: Reaction forces added at A and B; a given force misplaced; in the moments part most got one valid term, but the weakest resorted to trial and error rather than keeping d as a variable.
findings.rule: Keep the unknown distance as d in the moments equation and solve.

insight.ruleToRemember: Draw the rod's weight at its midpoint and every support or string force with its own label; take moments about a point where an unknown you do not want acts (clockwise = anticlockwise), keeping unknown distances as letters; resolve vertically; recalculate the reactions whenever a load changes.
insight.aStarSignal: Using both conditions together with a ratio or an unknown distance, and recalculating after the load changes.
